Interviewee: I, this, it comes back to me and, of course, before I was being—before I realized that they were throwing stones at me in the park. That was before that. I really thought it would be nice to join Hitler. I used to play with German soldiers, you know these little figurines. They looked just like...
Interviewer: The little toy soldiers.
Interviewee: Toy soldiers, toy soldiers. Of course, I had a Mercedes Benz, I guess. That's what Hitler drove around in. That open Mercedes Benz. I had that.
Interviewer: You mean a toy.
Interviewee: A toy, a Mercedes Benz. Where you know, a figure, an image of Hitler was—and SS troops you know. I played with those.
Interviewer: You had these toys...
Interviewee: I had these toys.
Interviewer: With an image of Hitler in...
Interviewee: An image of Hitler and an image of these SS troops and SA troops and what have you. And I was six years—I was seven years old.
Interviewer: These were the miniature—Were they iron or...
Interviewee: They were...
Interviewer: Or rubber?
Interviewee: What was it? What are they made of, like clay or not clay, it would break easy but...
Interviewer: They would break.
Interviewee: Yeah, probably iron. Probably iron, yeah. I don't know what happened to them.
Interviewer: Did your family know that you were playing with these?
Interviewee: Sure they did.
Interviewer: Did they say anything.
Interviewee: No, nothing until—No, I didn't, no, no not at my recollection.
Interviewer: Did they...
Interviewee: But then, like I said when I was seven, that was 1937. You figure 1937, we never thought it was—it would came to the Crystal like in Crystal Night and...
Interviewer: Did you have a sense of before then, that your parents were concerned about Hitler coming to power? That they were being affected?
Interviewee: Not really. Only I was concerned about that night, the Crystal Night and I didn't finish, actually as I was after...
Interviewer: No, please.
Interviewee: The way it happened, I went to school. Now that's when I really realized what was happening. I was going to school and, like I said, the synagogue was in, behind the school and the courtyard. So I visualize the courtyard and I seen the books and Torahs being in the middle of the courtyard, and the caretaker, he was not Jewish, he had a bloody face and, of course, there was no school, like I said. And that visualize and I never will forget that. The Torahs were on the courtyard. They weren't burned yet, but they were intending to burn. So I just went home right away and so then I realized that, and then, of course, at that time, my dad was in Dresden because he knew or he had the, what's it called hindsight?
Interviewer: He had foresight.
Interviewee: Foresight, I got mixed up.
Interviewee: He had his foresight that something is going to happen and...
Interviewer: How did it feel when you saw the Torahs in the courtyard? What was that feeling before you left, turned around and left?
Interviewee: The feeling, I really didn't have a feeling at that time because I didn't know the concept of the Torah, per se. We didn't really study the Torah or the—now, I afterwards, in China that where we really went into it—the Torah.
Interviewer: Was your family observant in anyway?
Interviewee: No, not too, no, not too observant. My dad did do the Friday night Kiddush. That's about it, but I never, no, no we weren't observant...
Interviewer: But you had a sense that these were holy books?
Interviewee: I had a sense that they were holy books, and I could not understand why they were thrown in the courtyard. I didn't have no conception why, why, you know? And until I was, like I said, I was eight years old then and finally—and why was this caretaker being injured, you know? I didn't have no, I, no conception at all, no conception at all.
Interviewer: When you went home, what happened?
Interviewee: I went home and my—you know something, it's kind of a blank because I was with disbelief that something like this can happen, I mean disbelief. And then I stayed home, I guess until—I never went back to that school again. Never went back to that school until we migrated to China. There was—it was shortly. My dad had, and anyway, my dad came back after it cooled down and I...
Interviewer: Were you worried about where he was at that point?
Interviewee: No, I thought he was on a business trip, but then it was, I was told to me later. They didn't tell me to keep, they didn't want to worry me too much, so they—you know it kind of reminded me, funny—it kind of reminded me of this movie Life is Beautiful, did you see that?
Interviewer: Yes.
Interviewee: And like I say, I, they made it so that everything is going to be ok. You know everything is no problems, you know. We'll go to it, try different places, to beautiful places. We go to Shangri-La, whatever and a...
Interviewer: So that's how your parents...
Interviewee: They believed that—as a matter of fact, my dad had an opportunity to go to South America. He had two opportunities, so that visa somehow did not come through yet, so they didn't want to wait. They didn't want to take any chances and Shanghai—well my uncle had, he was in the textile business in Germany. And he had a little money, and he helped my dad with a fare to come to China at that time, so, but South America never materialized.
Interviewer: And the South American plan was the only other plan that you know that your father might have pursued?
Interviewee: Yeah, yeah, it was Brazil, Brazil, as a matter of fact, he—Brazil or Bolivia. Now I'm not quite sure. One of these. Because I remember an uncle of mine went to Bolivia, ***. That's, I think it was Bolivia, because in Brazil they speak Portuguese. And I still have a Spanish-German dictionary at home. So it must have been Bolivia. It must have been Bolivia.
Interviewer: And when you got home, your mother was there?
Interviewee: Yeah, as I can recollect.
Interviewer: Did she explain anything to you?
Interviewee: Not really. No, that's what...
Interviewer: At that point? They really were protecting you.
Interviewee: Protecting me, exactly.
Interviewer: And it worked.
Interviewee: And it worked. With this kind of a mentality, we left China, with this kind of an attitude, so to speak. I had a ball. I mean my mother, I mean the anxiety of my parents, you see we had to cross, we left Germany, we...
Interviewer: When did you leave?
Interviewee: We left Germany April of 1939. As a matter of fact it was the day of Hitler's birthday.
Interviewer: April 20th?
Interviewee: No, April, I don't know what date it was, April, I think I have my dad's passport. I think it might be—and we had to cross Switzerland, we had to cross the Swiss-German border. Brenner, have you ever heard of that?
Interviewer: The Brenner Pass.
Interviewee: The Brenner Pass. And my mother—they were, they took a certain amount of jewelry with them and she was scared.
Interviewer: How were you traveling?
Interviewee: By rail. By rail and, like I say, I as a kid had a ball.
Interviewer: Do you remember any difficulty in...
Interviewee: No I didn't...
Interviewer:...in leaving?
Interviewee: No, no difficulty. When I went with my mother to get all these permits and visas and, from the German consulate. I went with my mother, and my mother never looked Jewish per se. So when I went with my mother, they took her first because they thought she was not Jewish. She was Jewish...
Interviewer: They thought she was German and not Jewish.
Interviewee: Exactly, and I, funny I remember that, and then I, later on I when she told me that they took her because she did not look I know—what is Jewish looking, I mean what is Jewish looking I mean, now a days it's kind of ridiculous, you know. But somehow you have this instinct of a refugee has a certain mannerism that you can just guess. Later on I can tell you a story where my guess was right, and they were refugees in California that I met. Their daughter I met here. It was a bizarre story.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: Ah.
Interviewer: So here you are on the train, with your parents?
Interviewee: With my parents going through the Brenner Pass...
Interviewer: Any brothers or sisters?
Interviewee: No, no I was the only one.
Interviewer: And your grandparents?
Interviewee: My grandparents, unfortunately, stayed behind, and they tried very hard to also get them out of there. See, you had them, the way I remember, they had an amount of business people and they arranged these trips. If you didn't have any money, you lost.
Interviewer: So you didn't, there wasn't family money to get your...
Interviewee: There was, if you had money, sure there was family, but there were certain people. You know, anybody that had a chance to get out of Germany, could get out.
Interviewer: To?
Interviewee: To wherever they wanted to go. At that time, of course, Shanghai was the only open port.
Interviewer: Yes.
Interviewee: Yeah, so but you still have to have a certain amount of money to get out of Germany.
Interviewer: So the fact that your grandparents didn't get out was a financial one?
Interviewee: No, it's just...
Interviewer: Is that what you're saying?
Interviewee:...well, I don't know. I really couldn't say but they were so close and yet so far away, when we were in Shanghai to get them out. My dad, my, like I said, my grandfather died of natural causes: then my grandmother somehow did...
Interviewer: She was deported.
Interviewee: She was deported later on. Where? We don't know. I assume it was Auschwitz, but where we don't know.
Interviewer: When did you find that out?
Interviewee: Well, after the war.
Interviewer: After the war.
Interviewee: After the war. Sure because they, my parents corresponded with my grandmother. It had to be proofread by German authorities, all letters that came went out of Germany.
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: Yeah, and they found out after the war. There's no trace of her. No trace.
Interviewer: So the train ride—Let's...
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer:...not lose the journey...
Interviewee: Ok, sure.
Interviewer:...was exciting.
Interviewee: To me it was.
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: Yeah. Not for my parents because they were full of anxiety.
Interviewer: Could you feel their anxiety?
Interviewee: Not really.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: I was so enthused about being on this train, and whenever I smell, what is it they put on these, tar. Whenever I smell tar, you go to any railway, when I—it kind of reminds me of my childhood. That's when I travel, and, yeah, no, it was a pleasant...
Interviewer: It's a pleasant...
Interviewee: A pleasant journey for me. To me it was. It was not a pleasant journey for my parents.
Interviewer: When...
Interviewee: But the anxiety of whether we were going to get through or not. See, they were afraid that something might go sour and then they might have to be deported back or something. But thank G-d...
Interviewer: When you talk about your parent's anxiety, when do you think you became aware of that? Of their anxiety, of what their concerns were?
Interviewee: Their anxiety?
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: I never really, I never felt that—I knew that they were afterwards, after the fact.
Interviewer: After the fact?
Interviewee: After the fact, you know, after the war.
Interviewer: After the war. As you look back.
Interviewee: As I look back. There are certain things that my mother told me.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: That I, that I know that they had to live full of anxiety even during the Shanghai ghetto.
Interviewer: But they were able to keep you optimistic during that time?
Interviewee: Yeah, oh yeah, definitely. I would say, I would even say, as far as I was concerned, that these were my best years of my life in, living in Shanghai, because I went to school, Shanghai Jewish Youth Association School, or Kadoorie School...
Interviewer: The Kadoorie School?
Interviewee:...And it was before the war. It was heaven for us. Of course the, the living standards were not up to par.
Interviewer: Let's, before we get to...
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Before we get to Shanghai...
Interviewee: Ok, we are, we're still on the train...
Interviewer: Let's talk about the train and make sure that we have all of these memories about that...
Interviewee: Ok, the train. We luckily—we passed the Brenner's Pass. Then we went through Italy and we ended up in Rome. And from Rome, I remember we took the train to Naples.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: And from Naples we boarded a shi—a combination passenger and freighter, a Japanese passenger and freighter—the Kaptori Mare and that took us to Shanghai.
Interviewer: Did it go directly to Shanghai? Did it make stops?
Interviewee: Yeah, it's no, no, no, it stopped in Bombay, and it stopped—it was a freighter. It took about four weeks from Naples to get to China.
Interviewer: Can you, I would love if you could describe that trip for me.
Interviewee: Oh that trip to me was like heaven. We were third class. See we had, it was a class, First Class, Second Class, Third Class. So we were Third Class. The only time, the only, what I remember the Second Class had a party. We were invited for this party. I don't know what kind of party, probably a cocktail party, whatever it was. It had Japanese waiters. Second—I mean people were traveling in style. They were not traveling they weren't traveling like refugees. They were traveling in style.
Interviewer: Were the people all refugees?
Interviewee: All refugees. All from Germany.
Interviewer: Ok. All German refugees.
Interviewee: Well, yeah that's, to my collection, yeah. And Austria, to Austria.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: Austria and Germany. And I remember I was sitting at the edge of the, where the, and I watched the entertainment. I was jealous, why can't we be there. We were Third Class. We were down a hole, you know, so to speak and by the, at the portholes, you know? And the Second Class they had very nice state rooms...
Interviewer: Oh my.
Interviewee:...And we had to share bunk beds. The women were separate and the men were separate. Not the Second Class. They were you know, men and women were together.
Interviewer: So you weren't in and just with your family? You were...
Interviewee: Yeah, oh, we were, well, my mother and women were in a separate cabin. You know, they have these wooden bunk beds. And as a matter of fact, one of the fellows—one of our passengers left the porthole open and water just shhhhish came down to—I was soaking wet and my dad, I guess he got mad and he had a few words with this individual who left the porthole open.
Interviewer: So you were with your father?
Interviewee: I was with my father.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: And another fellow, Dr., he was a medical doctor, Dr. Wolff. He was, I, funny I remember him and a...
Interviewer: Do you remember his first name?
Interviewee: No. Dr. Wolff and he gave me in, well that was later. All the diseases that was, that was meant, I mean that we were, we got in China—I had from malaria to typhus to typhoid and what have you, but mild, because we were inoculated, you see. We were inoculated.
Interviewer: Now before you were on the boat, was their any attempt to inoculate you? Or was there...
Interviewee: No, well we were inoculated in Germany, as I remember, you know for...
Interviewer: Before the...
Interviewee: For smallpox, yeah sure.
Interviewer: Now was this part of the regular regimen, or was this because of the trip?
Interviewee: Because of the trip.
Interviewer: So you were inoculated for smallpox.
Interviewee: For smallpox. They usual when you go overseas you know?
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: See my dad had a valid passport.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: That passport was good until 1941. I think that's what it says, I still have it here. So he was German, but he was Jewish, so there was a big "J" on it. But I mean, he could have gone with his passport anywhere in the world, providing they would...
Interviewer: Take him.
Interviewee: Take Germans.
Interviewer: Your mother had a passport as well.
Interviewee: Yeah, of course, yeah.
Interviewer: And what about you?
Interviewee: I didn't have a pass—I was with my mother's. On my mother's but I didn't have a picture. See they had a picture. So I was with my mother's, on my mother's passport.
Interviewer: Your name is...
Interviewee:...Because I was underage. I was not 10 years old.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: If I would have been 10 years and over, I would have had a passport also.
Interviewer: So you were not allowed, when you were on the boat, you were able to sneak up and view this very...
Interviewee: And view the Second Class, yeah.
Interviewer: But was there any kind of planned activity for the Third Class passengers or was it...
Interviewee: I don't remember. I...
Interviewer:...or was it informal?
Interviewee: It was very informal.
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: We just, the only activities that I remember were just cafeteria style, we ate, and the Second Class had their dining rooms.
Interviewer: Now in your family group, you had mentioned your uncle. Did he go with you?
Interviewee: No, not with us.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: He went, he went ahead of us...
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee:...to China. On a different boat. A lot of people went on Italian liners, and we had to go on a Japanese freighter.
Interviewer: What were the Japanese like who were running the boat?
Interviewee: Oh, they were terrific. They treated us just like regular passengers. And no, there was no ***. I did not know as a child, I did not know that they were at war with China already.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: And they gave us a beautiful—and I was so mad I had to give it up—beautiful Japanese flag, you know made out of silk.
Interviewer: Because you were on the boat?
Interviewee: On the boat, yeah. They all gave us one flag and, but they told us better not take it to China because they are at war. If somebody sees us with this Japanese flag, they might, who knows, you know? So I had to give it up and somebody else—you know that, excuse me, I think the boat went to China and, I think, went to Japan also.
Interviewer: You had to give it up before you left the boat.
Interviewee: I didn't have to give it up, but under the advisement of my parents...
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: No I didn't have to give it up.
Interviewer: I see.
Interviewee: Oh no.
Interviewer: I see. It was your parents' suggestion.
Interviewee: My parents suggestion, "You better!", I had no idea, no inkling why I had to give it up. But then I found out later on, then I realized they were at war with the Chinese since 1937.
Interviewer: Now when you...
Interviewee: So when...
Interviewee: Ok, now in Bombay, we stopped in Bombay. We stopped in Columbia. That's, isn't that Indonesia? *** was it also India. I cannot *** but I know in Columbia I was pic—I have a picture, I was pictured on a rickshaw, you know with the native. My mother was standing, and then in Singapore, Hong Kong, we stopped there.
Interviewer: So you were able to get off the ship and...
Interviewee: Of course. Yeah, yeah.
Interviewer: What...
Interviewee:...like tourist, like regular tourist.
Interviewer: What do you remember from those stops?
Interviewee: The stops? I remember in Singapore that people came up to the ship and tried to sell Persian carpets, and because they were a lot of Indians, too, East Indians. And there were a lot of, a lot of East Indians, as a matter of fact boarded, they boarded the—whether it was Bombay or Singapore, I cannot recollect—boarded the ship and they were—they booked to China. And as my recollection was, the British at that time used the East Indians for police in some sections. And we had a lot of East Indian Sikhs. They were policemen in China and they're nice people. And during the war, those Sikhs, one of the Sikhs came to the house and sold milk. They had their own cow, like Fiddler on the Roof, reminds me of. And it was expensive, very rare, my mother bought milk, but once in a while we use to get butter from this Indian family.
Interviewer: So these stops were positive? They were...
Interviewee: Oh yeah, definitely, yeah we were treated like tourists. And I was, as a child I had a ball.
Interviewer: What...
Interviewee: I did not, you know I was not old enough really to enjoy the concept of tourism cause I was just, you know...
Interviewer: Wide-eyed.
Interviewee:...just gazing all over. I mean with such an amazement.
Interviewer: Yes.
Interviewee: Such amazement. And I remember the carts in Hong Kong and Singapore and of course, Hong Kong, my conception of was very dirty and...
Interviewer: At the time, when you saw it?
Interviewee: Yeah, when I saw it. Also, Naples was very dirty. Naples, very dirty. And they had these carts and the donkeys and mules. Everyone had mules.
Interviewer: Had you any preconceptions about what these places would look like before you got there?
Interviewee: Not really, no. I did not.
Interviewer: So it was all very new...
Interviewee: Very new, very new, yeah. Like I said a lot of peop—I remember people came up to the ship and tried to sell Persian carpets. I remember, my parents never bought one. But they were, I remember we were to watch out for them. "They are conniving people. You had better watch out. And watch your money and watch your belongings, you know, when they come on board."
Interviewer: Were there other children that you met on the boat?
Interviewee: No, funny, you know, no, no, not really, not that I remember. I was the only, I was the only child, unless they had really infants but yeah, I was the only child. There were not too many passengers, cause it was a combination freighter. To me that was fascinating to watch them take the cargo off the ships and then loading the cargo back from all these places. To me, I was watching them for hours, to do that. I remember the noise of the cranes. As I'm speaking to you...
Interviewer: Yes.
Interviewee: I just, I never think about these things. Now that I am speaking to you, I remember the noises of the cranes, of these, you know, of these...
Interviewer: Fascinating machines...
Interviewee: Fascinating machines at that time, yes. Yes.
Interviewer: Could you, did you re-enact any of these things that you were seeing? Did you play on the boat?
Interviewee: I was, no, no. I was, it must come from these probably, when I lived in China, I use to have a board. It had a hole in it, kind of a—I use to put in underneath my bed, my bedsheet and I would pretend I was on a boat. I was in a porthole room. That was my porthole.
Interviewer: The board...
Interviewee: That was strange, the board, I have...
Interviewer: The next year yet...
Interviewee: I have the board like a, like a yeah. I put the cover over it, but there was enough space to see out, to see out in the room, you know? That was my little hide-a-way, that was my little boat...
Interviewer: Oh.
Interviewee: That was a, you know?
Interviewer: That was a safe place?
Interviewee: Safe place, exactly.
Interviewer: This boat...
Interviewee: That boat, how funny, funny, I never think about this, now with talking about, yeah...
Interviewer: So there was, you made a hole in the board?
Interviewee: No, no. It was already, it was already in there, you know two boards nailed together on a, I don't know what we used it for. To stand up on something, you know stand up like a, like a step stool more or less and I take this to bed and put, there was a space like this, you know?
Interviewer: Like a couple inches...
Interviewee: And I, yeah, a couple inches and that was my little hide-a-way, my little boat.
Interviewer: How long did you do that?
Interviewee: Maybe until I was, probably nine years, nine years or so. I still, yeah, I was crazy. That's what it was. Yeah, I felt safe there.
Interviewer: Very safe.
Interviewee: Very safe.
Interviewer: Did you think back to the boat at other times or was it, the board was...
Interviewee: The board was a...
Interviewer: Represents.
Interviewee:...a substitution of that boat, yeah. I was sad that the trip was over, in a way at that time. You know, but we could walk freer in China and freer, I mean you know there was other things that, other adventures that I remember I went with my cousin, I went to the wharves and watched the boats and come in and go out and...
Interviewer: Do you remember the day that you arrived in?
Interviewee: Yeah, the day was...
Interviewer: In Shanghai.
Interviewee: In Shanghai, it was in 19—well the day, we left in April so it took four weeks, so it must have been some time in May.
Interviewer: Of 1939?
Interviewee: Of 1939, yeah.
Interviewer: And can you tell me about the day that you arrived, what it was like.
Interviewee: The day that I arrived, I had to give up my flag, unfortunately.
Interviewer: Your parent's suggestion?
Interviewee: My parents suggested that I give this, because some people were going farther, were going to Japan...
Interviewer: Oh.
Interviewee: You see? Some of people were, yeah...
Interviewer: Some of the refugees were...
Interviewee: The refugees were going—then later on they had to come back but, and also there were a certain amount of Japanese passengers. And they went to Japan from—and that was my big disappointment, I had to give up the flag. And, I know, I do not have much recollection, as we got off the boat, the plank there, that—'cause what I see in pictures, they were being put on trucks, some of the refugees were put, and then they were going to a center, what is it called, the...
Interviewer: Where the refugee organizations were?
Interviewee: Yeah, I think HIAS1 and all these refugees organizations were interviewing, and people were sent to these—people who didn't have any money or didn't have any means of any, how should I say—they were sent to these homes, to these Heims, you know? To these...
Interviewer: But your family...
Interviewee: But my family, see, I do not remember. I'm trying to think because my uncle must have already bought the house because they were, oh yes, they were ahead of us. So they, he already had a house.
Interviewer: They meaning your uncle...
Interviewee: My uncle, my dad's brother.
Interviewer: Yes. And was any of his family?
Interviewee: Yeah, my cousins and his two kids were, my cousin, my male cousin and I had a female cousin, his sister, he had a sister. And...
Interviewer: They were about your age?
Interviewee: Yeah, my cousin is about one year older and his sister is about five years older than I.
Interviewer: And your aunt?
Interviewee: My aunt...
Interviewer: Was there?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: Yes, ok.
Interviewee: Sure. The whole family...
Interviewer: So this four, family of four was...
Interviewee: Of four, and then he rented out, we, each family had one room.
Interviewer: This is your father's brother.
Interviewee: Brother.
Interviewer: Ok.
Interviewee: He was in the textile business...
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee:...in Germany and he had a little bit money.
Interviewer: So he had a house...
Interviewee: He had a house. He bought a house on Seward Road, remember? You hear that so many times, you know.
Interviewer: Seward. Yes.
Interviewee: Seward Road.
Interviewer: And which section was Seward Road?
Interviewee: Hongkew.
Interviewer: In Hongkew. Ok.
Interviewee: We arrived. There was the occupation, there was Japanese occupation already. Some people left for the French Concession and the British, for the French, yeah, and the British settlement.
Interviewer: But your uncle had bought the house.
Interviewee: Bought a house in Hongkew, yeah. That was outside the, you know, the perimeter of the ghetto, so to speak.
Interviewer: What was it like? He, you got off the boat and you...
Interviewee: Well, the living standard, we had a—let's put it this way, we had all the conveniences of Western living. We had a WC, a regular bathroom and toilet, toilet, flushing toilet, and we—I went to, and then, of course, I was enrolled in the Kadoorie School later on, about a month or so, later on, I imagine. So, and then my, when on my ninth birthday, it was 1939, 1940. On my ninth birthday, my parents decided to enroll me into a religious school, just like you send your kids here to relig—to Sunday School. A relig...
Interviewer: A religious school.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: Before we go on to that, can you tell me whatever you remember about those early days. Do you think it's possible that your uncle met you at the boat, or do you remember how you got to Hongkew?
Interviewee: Yeah, I know—that's blank.
Interviewer: That's blank.
